content:
SSH keys are very widely used, for signing git commits, signing software distribution, authenticating with a remote server and age also supports encrypting files using SSH key pairs. It seems that SSH keys are the new PGP, only without the infamous web of trust and other stuff.

Security vulnerabilities are crazy these days. We have gaining root access with any password on musl linux , remote code execution hole on almost every server running PHP , Ubuntu not patching CVE-2026-98432 for more than half a month , RCE on OpenJDK , RCE on Ruby , Nginx2Root … NPM got weirdly quiet after swarms of supply chain attacks.

For individual developers, there are a lot of scary stories about fake job interviews stealing credentials with take-home projects. And people run arbitary code downloaded from the Internet all the time (e.g. package managers). It’s always a risk having your private keys sitting on your disk in plain text, especially in this environment where black hats have access to LLM agents to do evil things fast and in scale.

Better safe than sorry.

Passphrase is not strong enough

When you run ssh-keygen, you can optionally protect your private key with a passphrase, so every time you need to use that key (login to a server, sign a commit and etc.), you will be prompted to enter the passphrase. Even if attackers have successfully stolen your private key, they cannot gain access to your assets or steal your identity without the passphrase.

The thing is, it’s not really as hard to brute-force an SSH key as to brute-force a web service. There are no rate limits and attackers can do this concurrently. A passphrase can only buy you some time before they eventually crack into your system.

Keys should be disposable

You don’t want long-lived keys , because keys will eventually get exposed or lost, and when that happens, you need to replace them.

People normally use SSH key per device. For instance, if you have a work PC and a laptop and you want to login to your server on both of them, the common practice is to generate a key pair on each device.

When one device is lost, you still have access to your server on the other device, and you can remove the public key of the lost device so whoever has your device won’t be able to gain access to your assets.

By “keys should be disposable”, I mean you should prepare for cases like keys getting lost or exposed, have a backup plan and respond quickly. Usually that backup plan is an alternate key on another device.

Hardware-protected keys

Private keys stored as files are easily extractable. The advantage is that you can move your keys elsewhere and back it up. The downside is that attackers can also do that.

There’s such things as hardware-protected keys. They’re not files. You cannot copy them. An example is a physical key like YubiKey , which is a small pluggable device. YubiKey users normally generate a key pair directly into the device and the actual private key will never touch the local disk. What’s stored on your device is a public key and a “handle” that points to the physical key, so programs know they should ask the user to insert the actual key.

Well, if you have a Mac (Apple Silicon) and installed macOS Sequoia (and above), you don’t need an external device. Apple’s Secure Enclave is a secure subsystem isolated from the rest of the system, so no one can access it without your knowledge. You can configure it to authenticate with Touch ID every time you need to use it.

On how to set it up, you can read Serge Gatezh’s post . See the short version below:

  1. Create a Secure Enclave key. 
    sc_auth create-ctk-identity -l "ssh-MacBook" -k p-256-ne -t bio
    -t bio means it authenticates using Touch ID.
  2. Create a key handle 
    ssh-keygen -w /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib -K -N ""
  3. Move the handle to your ~/.ssh 
    mv id_ecdsa_sk_rk* ~/.ssh/
  4. Add this to your shell configuration (.zshrc, .bashrc, config.fish…) 
    export SSH_SK_PROVIDER=/usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib

    # fish
set -gx SSH_SK_PROVIDER /usr/lib/ssh-keychain.dylib
    And reload it or open a new shell session.

~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk is the key handle you use as a private key, except that it’s not really your private key. The actual key is in Secure Enclave. You can’t even export it yourself.

~/.ssh/id_ecdsa_sk_rk.pub is of course the public key, ssh-copyid it to your server, to your git forge and etc.

Beware the private key will be lost if you lost your Mac (just like how it would be lost if you lost your YubiKey). Keys are disposable. So always have backups.

My setup

I have 3 SSH key pairs.

  1. The primary key pair, stored in Secure Enclave.
  2. The secondary key pair, stored in my CanoKey (a cheaper YubiKey).
  3. The backup key pair, stored offline in an external hard drive.

All 3 public keys are stored on my device, and none of the private keys are.

Only the backup pair is exportable, but it’s almost never connected to the Internet. Unless someone had robbed me and also kidnapped me to force me to input my fingerprint and hand over the PIN number of my CanoKey (in that case I’d have something more important to worry about), my keys will be secure.

It feels smooth as well. All I have to do is to touch the top-right corner of my keyboard whenever I’m prompted (and sure of what I’m doing).

Extra: use with (r)age

aerc is my favourite Email client. It has Vim bindings and… well, that’s actually all I ask for.

The configuration is stored in plain text and so are my passwords. That’s definitely not secure. It’s recommended to use a password store like pass , which I choose to stay away from because it uses gpg… Yuck!

age is a simple, modern and secure encryption tool. It conveniently supports SSH keys.

The tricky part is that age does not natively support Secure Enclave key (nor YubiKey). You need to install a plugin.

  • age-plugin-se
  • age-plugin-yubikey

And this happened…

Error: age-plugin-se: no bottle available!
If no compatible bottle is available, you can try to install from source with:
 brew install --build-from-source age-plugin-se

OK, I will try building from source then…

age-plugin-se: This formula does not run on macOS versions older than Tahoe.
Error: age-plugin-se: An unsatisfied requirement failed this build.

Well, I hate Liquid Glass more. So I installed an older version of age-plugin-se and moved on. Hopefully I won’t have this kind of problems when I finally decided to move to GhostBSD .

Unfortunately my Canokey is not compatible with age-plugin-yubikey, so I’ll stick with age-plugin-se for now.

Generate a new key pair using age-plugin-se:

$ age-plugin-se keygen --access-control=any-biometry -o key.txt
Public key: age1se1qgg72x2qfk9wg3wh0qg9u0v7l5dkq4jx69fv80p6wdus3ftg6flwg5dz2dp

Save the public key and key.txt (private key). Encrypt your password and store it in a file. Here I’m using rage , a Rust implementation of age, because the Go implementation has Claude in it.

Ideally you should do this offline:

# encrypt eml_passwd and write to eml_passwd.age
rage -o eml_passwd.age -r pub.txt eml_passwd

Delete eml_passwd and continue.

For aerc to decrypt eml_passwd.age, edit ~/.config/aerc/accounts.conf.

source-cred-cmd = rage -d ~/.local/share/passwords/eml_passwd.age -i ~/.local/share/passwords/key.txt
outgoing-cred-cmd = rage -d ~/.local/share/passwords/eml_passwd.age -i ~/.local/share/passwords/key.txt

Now, when you open aerc or send a new email, you will be asked to use Touch ID, which is pretty cool.

Wish you were secure!
